title: The Place the LORD Will Choose
summary: The law code opens with worship. Israel must destroy the Canaanite shrines on hills and under trees and bring their sacrifices, tithes, and offerings only to the one place God will choose as a dwelling for his Name, where whole households will eat and rejoice before him. Ordinary meat may be slaughtered and eaten anywhere, as long as the blood is poured out, and Israel must never imitate the nations' worship, which included burning their children.
story: Chapters 6 to 11 called Israel to love the one God with all their heart. Chapter 12 begins the detailed laws of chapters 12 to 26, and it starts where that love most visibly takes shape: in worship. The first commandment said no other gods; this chapter adds that the one God must be worshiped in the way and at the place he chooses. The chapter never names that place. Later books show the ark and tabernacle at Shiloh (Joshua 18:1; Jeremiah 7:12) and then David bringing the ark to Jerusalem and Solomon building the temple there, so that the books of Kings judge each king by whether he protected the one sanctuary or tolerated the high places. The theme of the chosen place runs all the way to Jesus' words about true worship.
historical:
This chapter stands at the center of modern debates about Deuteronomy. Since the nineteenth century many scholars have linked it with the reforms of King Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:4) and especially King Josiah of Judah, who in about 622 BC removed the high places throughout the land and brought worship to Jerusalem alone (2 Kings 23). On this view, the law of the one place was written or given its final shape to support that reform. Others hold that the principle is older: they point out that the chapter never names Jerusalem and could have applied first to Shiloh or whatever site housed the ark, and that Israel's earlier history already shows a central sanctuary alongside other altars. Archaeology has contributed without settling the question. At Arad in the Negev, excavators found a small Judahite shrine with an altar and standing stones, which some date to the eighth century and connect with Hezekiah's reform, though its dating and history are debated.

The practice of child sacrifice named in verse 31 is condemned repeatedly in the Old Testament, which reports that the kings Ahaz and Manasseh of Judah made their sons pass through the fire (2 Kings 16:3; 21:6) and that the king of Moab sacrificed his son on the city wall during a siege (2 Kings 3:27).
cultural:
Canaanite religion, like much ancient worship, was local. Shrines stood on hilltops, which were thought to be closer to the gods, and under leafy trees, which were linked with fertility. Each town and region could have its own altar, its own standing stones, and its own version of the god. Moses commands the opposite: one sanctuary for the whole nation, chosen by God rather than by human preference. This protected Israel from blending their God with local deities and from turning worship into whatever each clan thought best, which is the meaning of verse 8, "everyone does what seems right in his own eyes."

In the ancient world nearly all meat was eaten in connection with sacrifice. Once worship was centered in one place, families living far away would rarely be able to eat meat at all. Verses 15 and 20 to 25 allow ordinary slaughter at home, treating a sheep or ox like a gazelle or deer (wild animals never offered as sacrifices). The one rule that remains is the blood. Because "the blood is the life" (verse 23), it belongs to God and must be poured on the ground. Worship at the chosen place was also a feast: offerings were eaten by the family with servants and Levites, and the chapter repeatedly commands joy.
literary: The chapter is framed by warnings not to worship the LORD in the nations' way (verses 4 and 31) and by the command to do exactly as God says (verses 1 and 32). Inside that frame, the law of the one place is stated several times with variations (verses 5 to 7, 11 and 12, 13 and 14, 17 and 18, 26 and 27). Some scholars see these as layers from different periods; others see a typical pattern of ancient legal teaching, repeating and expanding a principle to cover different situations. The key phrase is "the place the LORD your God will choose," which recurs throughout Deuteronomy's law code. The chapter's last verse, forbidding additions or subtractions, echoes 4:2.

outline.t: Destroy the nations' places of worship
Worship at the one place God will choose
Meat may be eaten anywhere; sacred gifts only at the sanctuary
Eating meat far from the sanctuary, and the blood
Do not imitate the nations' worship

doctrines.note: Idolatry is not only worshiping other gods; it can also mean worshiping the true God in the ways of false religion. "You shall not worship the LORD your God in this way" (verse 4) warns against shaping God's worship by borrowed practices and personal preference.

God chooses the place and the manner of his worship. His Name dwells where he decides, and Israel approaches him on his terms. Holiness here protects the people from turning God into a local deity they can manage.

Blood is forbidden as food because "the blood is the life" (verse 23). Leviticus 17:11 explains that God gave blood on the altar to make atonement. Pouring it out honored the life that belonged to God and prepared for the sacrificial system that the New Testament sees fulfilled in Christ.

words.note: Maqom, place. It appears nine times in the chapter and becomes almost a title: "the place the LORD your God will choose." The word can simply mean a location, but here it means the site God claims for his presence. The refusal to name it kept the focus on God's choice rather than on any city's prestige.

Shakan, to dwell or settle. God chooses a place to make his Name dwell there (verse 5 and 11). From this verb comes the word mishkan, tabernacle, and later Jewish writers used a related term for God's dwelling presence. The phrase affirms that God is truly present without implying he is confined to a building.

Dam, blood. The ban on eating blood goes back to God's word to Noah (Genesis 9:4) and is repeated in Leviticus 17. It marks the difference between using an animal for food and taking its life, which belongs to God alone.

Samach, to rejoice. Worship at the chosen place is commanded as a joyful feast shared by family, servants, and Levites (verses 7, 12, and 18). Deuteronomy consistently treats gladness before God as part of obedience, not an optional extra.

christ: John's Gospel says the Word became flesh and "made His dwelling among us," using a Greek verb that echoes the tabernacle, where God made his Name dwell (John 1:14). When the Samaritan woman asked whether God should be worshiped on Mount Gerizim or in Jerusalem, Jesus said the hour was coming when true worshipers would worship the Father in spirit and truth, not tied to one mountain (John 4:21-24). The New Testament presents Jesus himself as the place where God meets his people. He speaks of his body as a temple (John 2:19-21), and after his resurrection the church, gathered in his name, becomes God's dwelling by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:21-22). The chapter's concern that God be worshiped on his terms, not ours, carries into the New Testament, but the one place is no longer a city. It is a person.
questions: Moses warns against worshiping God in the ways the nations worshiped their gods. What habits or assumptions from the wider culture might shape the way people approach God without their noticing?
The chapter commands rejoicing before God with family, servants, and Levites. How might worship change if joy and shared meals were treated as part of obedience?
Verse 8 describes a time when everyone did what seemed right in his own eyes. In what areas are you most tempted to follow your own judgment rather than God's word?
